children.text: The old heart of downtown Cebu, known as the oldest street in the Philippines. Along its roughly
1.2 km

run you'll find an obelisk and historical markers, old theater buildings, budget malls and street stalls, and in night market season it stays busy until late, giving you a close look at everyday life in Cebu.
Colon Street is the old main street of downtown Cebu City, running east to west for about
1.2 km

. It starts at the obelisk on P. Burgos Street at its eastern end, passes the big intersection with Osmeña Boulevard, and continues west to C. Padilla Street. The name comes from Cristóbal Colón, the Spanish name of Christopher Columbus, and locals simply call it "Colon." Today it is a working-class street packed with budget malls, clothing and phone shops, street stalls and jeepneys squeezed between aging commercial buildings.
The street is widely known as "the oldest street in the Philippines." In
the national historical agency put up a marker reading "Also known as the Parian, the oldest street in the Philippines. Built in
," and in
it added a Filipino-language marker on the obelisk.
is the year Miguel López de Legazpi founded the Spanish settlement in Cebu. Cebu historian Jobers Bersales, however, points out that on a
map Colon lay outside the early Spanish town, and that the reputation spread after a Cebu shop sold postcards in
labeled "Oldest Street in Cebu." He considers Magallanes Street, which runs past Magellan's Cross, to be the older street. The oldest map that actually shows Colon also dates from
, so "the oldest street" is better understood as a story told for over a century than as settled fact.
Still, there is no doubt Colon was the stage for Cebu's modern history. From the
to the
it was the city's center of commerce and entertainment. Theaters such as Teatro Junquera (later Cine Oriente), completed in
, along with the Vision, Eden and Ideal, lined the street together with department stores and offices, and in

the Visayan Institute moved here, becoming today's main campus of the University of the Visayas. Later, as large malls and new business districts rose in the suburbs, the crowds drifted away and the old theaters became shops or wholesale stores. Plans to revive the street as a pedestrian zone have come up several times but have not been carried out.

If you expect a tidy tourist attraction, you may be disappointed. Exhaust fumes and noise, worn buildings, tangled power lines and crowded sidewalks are Colon's real face. In return, you can buy cheap clothes and goods, snack on street food, and hunt for old theater facades and historical markers while watching Cebu's daily life up close.
Basilica del Santo Niño
and
Carbon Market
are about
10 minutes
away on foot, making it easy to combine with a walking tour of the old town, and in night market season it also makes a good evening outing.
At the eastern end of the street, where it meets P. Burgos Street, stands a gray obelisk with a
Filipino-language marker on its base. A little farther west, an English marker from
remains on the pillar of an old building. Early morning, when traffic is light, is a good time for photos.

blocks.title: Vision Theater and old theater sites

children.text: Near the Osmeña Boulevard intersection stands the Vision Theater building, built in the
. Its tall vertical VISION sign and the sculpted decoration on the upper facade survive, and the building made it through the bombing of
. Today shops occupy the ground floor while the upper floors are run-down, so it is best viewed from across the street. The nearby Colonnade Mall stands where Cine Oriente used to be.

Metro Colon, Gaisano Capital South, Colonnade Mall, 138 Wholesale Mall (which promises "retail purchase, wholesale price") and Iconique Mall are all within a few blocks. Clothes, shoes, bags and household goods cost less than at suburban malls, so it's a good place to pick up shorts or sandals you forgot to pack. Metro Colon reopened after a renovation in
July 2026
Small shops and arcades are crammed wall to wall with phone cases, charging cables, earphones, caps and bags. Prices are low but quality varies, so plug things in and test them before you buy.

Ukay-ukay are shops that sell piles of imported secondhand clothing, and Colon is one of Cebu's well-known ukay-ukay streets. With some digging you can find shirts or jackets in good condition for very little, and young locals sift through the piles as if on a treasure hunt.
This night market began in
to revive the street. Each year in the second half of the year, part of the street is closed to traffic and hundreds of tent stalls set up, selling street food, clothes and sundries. In
it opened in
September
, with traffic closed from
6:30 PM to 2:00 AM

. Permits have been disputed. The 2026 season is also reported to run from early September to around Sinulog in January, but the days and operating or closure hours differ between reports, so check the latest announcements.

Around sunset, flocks of small swiftlets fly in and settle densely on the power lines and old buildings of Colon and nearby streets. The sight of them darkening the sky is worth seeing, but standing right under the wires is a good way to get hit by droppings, so watch from a little to the side.

items.title: Morning history walk
items.subtitle: Markers, old theaters and the old town

children.text: Start at the obelisk at the eastern end. Read the markers and take photos while traffic is light.
Walk west to see the
marker on an old building's pillar and the main campus of the University of the Visayas.
From across the street, look at the former Cine Oriente site in front of Colonnade Mall and the facade decoration of the Vision Theater building.
Browse clothes and sundries at Metro Colon and 138 Wholesale Mall once they open, and buy what you need.
Walk south along Osmeña Boulevard to visit the Basilica del Santo Niño and Magellan's Cross.
Have lechon and puso for lunch at a downtown restaurant, and if you have time, walk on to Carbon Market.
Look around the Basilica del Santo Niño first, then walk along Osmeña Boulevard toward Colon.
Photograph the obelisk and the street at dusk and watch the swiftlets gather on the power lines.
Once the road closes to traffic, stroll between the night market tents, have grilled skewers and snacks for dinner, and browse the clothing and sundries stalls.
Head out to a busy main road and call a Grab or a metered taxi back to your hotel.
Outside night market season, shops pull down their shutters early after sunset and the street goes dark. At those times, choose the morning route instead of the evening one.
Flights from Manila to Mactan-Cebu International Airport (CEB) take about
1 hour 20 minutes
, with several daily departures on Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific. From South Korea there are direct flights from Incheon, Busan and other cities (about
4 hours 30 minutes
From the airport to Colon by taxi takes about
40 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes
depending on traffic, and costs about
. With Grab you can see the fare in advance.
From hotels around IT Park or Ayala Center it takes about
20–40 minutes
and costs about
. Drivers will understand "Metro Colon" or "Colon Obelisk" as a destination.
The area around the Osmeña Boulevard intersection is always congested and there are few places to stop. It's faster to get out a block away and walk in.

Many of Cebu City's jeepneys pass through Colon or start here. Take one with "Colon" on the windshield, such as the 13C from Talamban; routes like 01K and 14D also pass Colon. Look at the route code on the windshield rather than the destinations painted on the side.
Since
September 28, 2026
, the fare for the first
4 km
is
on a traditional jeepney and
on a modern jeepney. Have coins and small change ready, and when you want to get off, say "lugar lang" and the driver will stop. Route codes and fares may change.
Buses from southern Cebu, such as Oslob, Moalboal and Carcar, arrive at the Cebu South Bus Terminal on N. Bacalso Avenue. From the terminal to the western end of Colon is about
, around
10 minutes
on foot. Take a taxi if you have a lot of luggage.
From the Basilica del Santo Niño and Magellan's Cross, walk about
north along Osmeña Boulevard,
7–10 minutes
, to reach the Colon intersection. From Carbon Market it is also about
10 minutes
on foot.
From Fort San Pedro to the obelisk at the eastern end is about
, roughly
15 minutes
on foot, so it's easy to walk together with the other old town sights. Walking the street end to end at a relaxed pace takes
15–20 minutes
Fast ferries from Bohol reach Cebu's port in about
2 hours
, and from the pier to Colon is about
10 minutes
by taxi. In 2026 cancellations and schedule changes have been frequent because of maintenance and fuel costs, so check the ferry company's notices for schedules and the arrival pier.
The street is open all year, but the best time for walking is the
December–May
dry season.
December–February
brings relatively cool mornings and evenings, while in
March–May
midday temperatures often exceed
and the shadeless sidewalks get very hot. In that period, walk early in the morning or around sunset and spend the midday hours inside the air-conditioned malls.
During the
June–November
rainy season, showers are frequent and heavy rain quickly floods downtown streets. As during Typhoon Tino in
November 2025

, the whole of Metro Cebu can flood, so postpone your visit if a typhoon warning is issued. The night market usually opens in the second half of the year and runs through the year-end, and on weekends in
December
Christmas shoppers pour in. Every year around the third Sunday of
January
, during the Sinulog festival, downtown roads are closed and the streets fill with processions and crowds.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Around Colon and the southern end of Osmeña Boulevard there are many older business hotels and pension houses at about

a night, within walking distance of the old town sights. However, on nights without the night market the shops close early and the streets turn dark and quiet, so it isn't recommended for first-time visitors. If it's your first trip, staying at a hotel around IT Park or Ayala Center (about
), with plenty of restaurants and malls, and commuting
20–40 minutes
by taxi is more relaxing. You can also stay at a resort on Mactan Island and come into the city for just half a day.

Street snacks eaten standing up are the real taste of Colon. Try banana cue (sugar-coated fried bananas), fried fish ball skewers, charcoal-grilled pork barbecue, ngohiong (Cebu-style fried spring rolls) and siomai, buying a piece at a time from the stalls. Instead of plain rice, Cebuanos eat puso, rice cooked in a woven coconut-leaf pouch. If you'd rather sit down, there are mall food courts, Filipino chains like Jollibee and Mang Inasal, and carinderias, where you pick rice and dishes from a counter, all along the street.

Cebu's signature dish, lechon (charcoal-roasted whole pig), makes a good lunch with puso at a downtown restaurant. For a proper evening of charcoal-grilled skewers, the Larsian barbecue alley near Fuente Osmeña, about
2 km
to the north, is about
10 minutes
away by taxi. In night market season, the stalls on Colon Street also sell grilled skewers and street food until late.
Take photos of the historical markers and old buildings early in the morning when there are fewer cars and people, and shop after the stores and malls open. Weekday mornings are the least crowded.
Most small shops and stalls accept cash only. They often can't break
bills, so bring plenty of
notes.

Bargaining is normal at stalls and small shops without price tags. Compare prices at a few places, then buy several items together and ask with a smile for a small discount. At fixed-price stores inside malls, pay the marked price.
Board jeepneys by the route code on the windshield; fares are passed forward through the passengers to the driver. When your stop is near, say "lugar lang."
Colon, the Basilica del Santo Niño, Magellan's Cross, Fort San Pedro and Carbon Market are all within
15 minutes
of each other on foot, so you can cover them all in half a day. Plan your walking order to avoid the heat.
Whether and when the night market opens differs every year. Before you go, check Cebu City announcements or local media such as SunStar and Cebu Daily News.

Colon Street and the surrounding downtown have long been known as an area of Cebu City where pickpocketing and phone snatching are common. Thieves especially target people getting on and off jeepneys after dark and crossing crowded intersections. In
September 2026

, ahead of the year-end rush, Cebu City police also stepped up patrols around commercial areas, markets and terminals and warned the public about pickpockets. Wear your bag in front with the zipper closed, don't walk with your phone in your hand, and keep your back pockets empty.
During night market season, on weekends in
December
and during Sinulog in
January
, crowds swell and thefts of belongings increase. Carry only the cash and valuables you need, and leave expensive watches and jewelry at your hotel.
On nights without the night market, the shops are closed and the street is dark and quiet. Don't go into unlit side streets, and get a Grab or metered taxi from a main road to head back.

Cheap chargers, power banks and electronics bearing famous brand names include fakes and defective goods. Because of the risk of overheating, test them on the spot, and buy anything you'll charge for long periods at your hotel from a reputable store.
Sidewalks are narrow and stalls block the way, so it's easy to get pushed into the road. Jeepneys and motorcycles pass constantly, so cross with the signals and don't stop in the road to take photos.

The upper floors of old buildings such as the Vision Theater are run-down. Don't enter buildings that are closed off, and politely decline people who approach you on the street offering money exchange or goods.
